catalog_quote: III. Accent tonique. L'accent tonique a un rôle important, car certains mots en tout semblables pour l'orthographe ont des sens tout à fait différents d'après l'accent tonique. Ex.: maina = huile de palme; maína = belle-sœur; djabá = tabac; djába = traverse (une rivière) du verbe kadjaba, traverser. D'autres fois tout en prononçant correctement les lettres d'un mot on n'est pas compris, parce qu'on ne met pas l'accent tonique, où il faut. C'est difficile de former des règles fixes concernant l'accent tonique. Elles seraient trop nombreuses et toujours avec trop d'exceptions. L'expérience et l'habitude doivent servir de maître.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.translation: III. Tonic accent. The tonic accent plays an important role, for certain words entirely alike in spelling have quite different meanings according to the tonic accent. Ex.: maina = palm oil; maína = sister-in-law; djabá = tobacco; djába = (he) crosses (a river), from the verb kadjaba, to cross. At other times, even while pronouncing the letters of a word correctly, one is not understood because one does not put the tonic accent where it should be. It is difficult to form fixed rules concerning the tonic accent. They would be too numerous and always with too many exceptions. Experience and habit must serve as teacher.
new_statements.citation: Gérard, [R. P.] (S.C.J.). 1924. La langue lebéo: grammaire et vocabulaire. (Bibliothèque Congo 13.) Bruxelles: A. Vromant & Co.

(1) Quote: the p. 11 page scan of Gerard 1924 'La langue lebeo' (Google Books full-view copy ZfVB30sGt1YC, header 'NOTIONS PRELIMINAIRES 11') carries the section 'III. Accent tonique.' and the passage exactly as quoted: 'L'accent tonique a un role important, car certains mots en tout semblables pour l'orthographe ont des sens tout a fait differents d'apres l'accent tonique. Ex.: maina = huile de palme; maina [acute on i] = belle-soeur; djaba [acute on final a] = tabac; djaba [acute on first a] = traverse (une riviere) du verbe kadjaba, traverser. D'autres fois tout en prononcant correctement les lett…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Per Gérard, the position of the 'accent tonique' is a lexical property of each word: it distinguishes segmentally identical words (maina vs maína, djabá vs djába) and cannot be reduced to positional rules. In verb derivation the accent stays on the root syllable of the simple verb (applicative -e-), except that the inserted applicative allomorphs -éle-/-néle- and the long particle lēa carry the accent, and in causatives the stem-final i before inserted h receives it (naéngia 'I enter' vs naengí-h-a 'I make enter'). Caveat: this is a 1924 pre-tonological missionary description of a Bantu C40 (Bwa-bloc) language; the 'accent' minimal pairs almost certainly reflect lexical tone (the Bwa bloc languages are two-tone languages, cf. Boone & Olson 2004), so the statement should not be read as evidence of a genuine lexical stress system.
new_statements.exceptions: p. 70: 'L'accent tonique reste sur la syllabe du verbe simple' in applicatives; -éle-/-néle- 'porteront aussi l'accent tonique'; applicative -lea has short unaccented e, whereas the tense particle lēa is long 'et par conséquent portera l'accent'; p. 72: causative with inserted h, 'i reçoit l'accent tonique'; p. 10: y = i before a vowel 'quand il n'a pas l'accent'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (citation forms of nouns and fully inflected verb words such as nadêta, naengí-h-a); accent marked with an acute on the vowel in Gérard's examples. No distinction drawn between pitch and intensity; no phrase-level discussion.
new_statements.identity_note: Gérard describes 'Lebéo', the language of the Babéo, i.e. the people the Wangwana/Europeans call (Wa)ngbelima / Bangelima / Mongelima, on the lower Aruwimi (Lohale) between Yambuya-Banalia and Panga; Van Bulck 1948 files the grammar under 'LeAngba des BAngba' within the MoNgelima (BaHanga, BaBindja, MoGandjo, BaBoro, BAngba) cluster. This is Ngelima/Angba proper = ngel1238 (Guthrie C45; Motingea 2009 labels it lebéo-ngelema C44/C45). The Kisangani theses on the list of works to obtain treat a specific variety, lehangá (Hanga), of the same language.

new_statements.translation: III. Tonic accent. The tonic accent plays an important role, for certain words that are identical in spelling have entirely different meanings according to the tonic accent. E.g. maina = palm oil; maína = sister-in-law; djabá = tobacco; djába = cross (a river), from the verb kadjaba, to cross. At other times, even pronouncing the letters of a word correctly, one is not understood, because one does not put the tonic accent where it belongs. It is difficult to form fixed rules concerning the tonic accent. They would be too numerous and always with too many exceptions. Experience and habit must serve as teacher. [p. 70:] N.B. The tonic accent stays on the syllable of the simple verb.

new_statements.relation_note: Same statement as existing_statements (Gérard 1924 p. 11, 'lexical (unpredictable)'); fills the empty rule of the catalog record 'Lebéo' (world-2026-09-17). Adds the derived-verb placement remarks (pp. 70, 72) as refinement. Pre-tonological 1924 description: the 'accent tonique' minimal pairs are almost certainly lexical tone (Lebéo is a C40 Bantu language; the SIL Bwa-bloc survey held by the project notes tone contrasts for Ngelima), so the modern reading would be tonal rather than stress. Today's fresh download of pp. 5-9 and 12 failed (HathiTrust not reachable by automated download/'Blocked', Google Books 403 'Sorry'), but the TOC snippet shows the accent section is only p. 11, which was…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Accent placement is not rule-governed: it distinguishes otherwise identical words (maina/maína, djabá/djába), the author declines to state rules ('too numerous, too many exceptions'). Morphological stability in derived verbs: the applicative keeps the accent on the syllable of the simple verb (p. 70 N.B.), except that the long extensions -ele-/-nele- and the long -lea- carry the accent (p. 70 Rem. 1-2), and the causative infix -i(h)- after a vowel 'reçoit l'accent tonique' (p. 72 Rem. 2). The p. 5 search snippet ('l'accent tonique est sur « é » et non sur l'avant-dernière syllabe « li » comme cela devrait être en Kiswaheli') concerns the Swahili-style ethnonym Wangbélima, not Lebéo words.
new_statements.exceptions: Author states rules would have 'trop d'exceptions' and gives none as such; derived-verb remarks (p. 70, 72) are the only placement statements: applicative -e- does not move the accent, but -ele-/-nele- and long -lea- take it (short -lea- does not, to keep it distinct from the long tense particle -lea-); causative -i(h)- takes the accent.
new_statements.identity_note: Gérard 1924 describes 'lebéo', the language of the Babeo (Bangba / Bangelima, 'Wangbélima' in the Swahili-derived name) on the Lohali-Aruwimi, Belgian Congo — the variety Glottolog files as Ngelima/Angba (ngel1238, Bantu C45). No dialect is singled out.
